articles.title_orig: Man who died after being ‘ejected’ from Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia was cherished teacher, school says
articles.title_zh: Man who died after being ‘ejected’ from Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia was cherished teacher, school says
articles.content_orig:
• Victim identified: The man who died after being “ejected” from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia yesterday has been identified by police as Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, of Atlanta, a charter school IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach. Several others were also injured.
• Eyewitness accounts: Witnesses said Kariem struck several other people before falling beneath the ride, according to police. The manufacturer of the ride said it is “actively investigating the incident” and Six Flags temporarily closed at least 10 roller coasters across several of its parks in the US and Canada.
• CNN investigation: The tragedy comes two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it would permanently close its world-famous ride X2 following a CNN investigation that documented reports of life-altering injuries and deaths.
A man who fell to his death from a roller coaster at an Atlanta-area amusement park was not the first to die on such a ride in recent years.
Authorities have not released information about how 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was thrown from Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Several people also were injured.
Here’s a look at other fatalities and injuries on US roller coasters:
The park in Southern California announced last month that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to a hospital with severe brain bleeding in 2022. He died a day later. Six Flags Entertainment Corp. said the ride had consistently passed safety tests.
A medical examiner concluded last year that a man who was unresponsive after riding a roller coaster at the Universal Orlando Resort park died from blunt impact injuries. Joshua Stephany, the medical examiner for the Orlando area, ruled the death an accident.
In 2013, a woman riding a roller coaster in Texas died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 75 feet and struck a metal beam. Witnesses said the woman expressed concern about the Texas Giant roller coaster’s safety bar not completely engaging as the ride was starting.
A US Army veteran who lost both legs in Iraq was killed in 2011 after he was thrown from a roller coaster at Darien Lake Theme Park & Resort in upstate New York. Investigators said operators did not follow rules posted at the ride’s entrance, which require that riders have both legs.
A 21-year-old rider fell to her death from a roller coaster at the amusement park in Louisiana in 2010. A state investigation could not determine a cause.
In 2003, a locomotive broke loose from a train on the Big Thunder Mountain Railroad roller coaster in California, killing a man and injuring multiple other riders. The car derailed after a guide wheel fell off. State investigators found the wheel was not tightened according to Disney’s standards and a safety wire was not installed.
The man who died after reportedly falling off a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia yesterday was “a cherished member” of Wesley International Academy, an Atlanta public charter school, Atlanta Public Schools said in a statement.
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was Wesley International Academy’s IT manager, a technology teacher and robotics coach, the school said.
Kariem’s “presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched,” the school district said. “Atlanta Public Schools extends its deepest condolences to the family, friends, and loved ones of Mr. Kariem.”
He was with the district for over 12 years, a spokesperson said.
“Our thoughts are with everyone mourning his loss during this difficult time,” the statement said.
The federal government has no regulation over amusement park rides, rather that responsibility is left to the states.
Mobile amusement rides, like those at a carnival, are regulated by the Consumer Product Safety Commission, but “fixed-site rides,” like the ones at Six Flags, are outside of the commission’s jurisdiction .
This came after Congress passed the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 , limiting the commission’s oversight only to rides not permanently fixed to the site and leaving it to states to regulate amusement park rides.
There is no uniformity across the country over which state regulator is in charge of inspecting amusement park rides. For example, the Texas Department of Insurance takes the lead that state, whereas in California, it falls under the state Department of Industrial Relations .
This web of state-by-state regulations have received backlash, especially by Sen. Ed Markey , who has repeatedly introduced legislation to return the oversight of amusement park rides to the CPSC, and calling the current legislation a “loophole” in safety regulations.
The Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire is starting an investigation after a man fell off the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia and died, the office said in a statement.
The first Six Flags amusement park, Six Flags Over Texas, opened its gates in 1961 after real estate developer Angus Wynne Jr. envisioned the park as a temporary use for the land before developing it into an industrial complex.
The park was designed to celebrate Texas’ history, and its name refers to the nations whose flags had flown over the state: Spain, France, Mexico, Texas, the United States and the Confederacy.
It wasn’t until 2017 that Six Flags decided to stop flying the Confederate Flag over its amusement parks, The Washington Post reported.
The flags represent the “changes, complexities, and richness found throughout the state’s history,” according to the Bullock Texas State History Museum , but fail to recognize the long-standing history of Indigenous people who dominated the region.
Wynne Jr. later sold Six Flags and the company was eventually expanded. Today, Six Flags is the largest regional theme park company in the world.
The Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire is starting an investigation after a man fell off the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia and died, the office said in a statement.
“Our investigative team is conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident and to ensure full compliance with all applicable policies and procedures,” the statement said.
The agency is responsible for overseeing inspections of amusement and carnival rides for safety, which are completed before a ride goes into service. Annual inspections are also required, according to the office’s website.
Six Flags says various teams perform extensive maintenance and inspections to keep its rides running safely. But what qualifications do the employees operating the rides need?
Six Flags currently lists various ride operator positions throughout the country, with similar requirements and qualifications across locations.
Applicants must be at least 16 years old, with hourly pay ranging from $12 in Texas to $17.50 in California .
A current listing for a rides team member in Austell, Georgia, a role with similar qualifications and responsibilities to a ride operator, pays $11.50 per hour.
Some of the daily functions of an operator include performing daily equipment checks before the ride opens to the public and confidently operating rides “using controls, signals, and communication.”
Operators are also responsible for pressing buttons and switches to start the rides and ensuring restraints have been checked and secured, according to several of the postings.
Ride operators must also pass ride certification tests with 100% accuracy.
Six Flags says its rides are engineered with safety systems and that each attraction has unique requirements.

articles.title_orig: China's exports likely grew by double-digits in September
articles.title_zh: China's exports likely grew by double-digits in September
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — China's exports likely grew by 25.5% in September from a year ago, picking up modestly from the prior month, according to a Reuters poll ahead of the expected Wednesday data release.
Imports for September were forecast to slow to 24.5% year-on-year growth, down from 28.2% in August, the poll showed.
Earlier this year, China's exports and imports each grew at their fastest pace in five years.
A surge in demand for China-made parts for data centers to power artificial intelligence has helped fuel exports, along with stabilization in tensions with the U.S., China's largest trading partner on a single-country basis.
Global scrutiny on the economic impact of China's surging exports has escalated in recent years , amid sluggish domestic demand. AI-related demand and a coinciding rise in prices of core products have also helped support import growth.
The U.S. and China last month announced plans to roll back tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, and extend a broader trade truce by two months to January.
The European Union last week announced China agreed to halve its exports of hybrid-powered cars to the bloc, following high-level trade talks in Beijing.

Investigation into Jiin Ming Industry is the second in two months over prohibited mainland gear in military drones

articles.title_orig: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.title_zh: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.content_orig:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
articles.content_orig:
An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday.
The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated.
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."
Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures , a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later.
The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta , Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT.
Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance."
Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room.
The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room.
The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device."
The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ.
This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems.
Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI."
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article.

articles.title_zh: Your Quick Primer on Katie Zacharia’s False Claim to Have Taken the Bar in China
articles.content_orig:
Katie Zacharia worked at a Beijing law firm and calls herself a lawyer, but reporters found no record of her admission to practise in the US
Katie Zacharia, US President Donald Trump’s newly appointed White House press secretary, faces questions about her legal credentials after telling reporters on Tuesday that she passed a bar exam “when I moved to China”, without identifying the jurisdiction.
A review by the South China Morning Post of attorney registration records in New York, the District of Columbia, California, Texas and Florida found no listing for Zacharia.
Independent journalist Judd Legum separately reported finding no evidence that she had been admitted to practise law in any of the 50 US states or Washington, DC.

articles.title_orig: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
articles.title_zh: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs.
The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research, said on a podcast that the investment bank published Tuesday.
Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, to accelerate plans for entering other countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans to enter Canada next year .
Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners.
Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors.
Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance.
Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years.
That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said.
But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%.
The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors.
"Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. "Brands are becoming long-term, embedded competitors capable of reshaping market dynamics across Latin America.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV arrives at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, where doctors operated to remove part of his lung. Alessandra Tarantino/AP hide caption
Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.
The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.
Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.
The Pope's surgery, which the doctors said was successful, lasted about 90 minutes, after which Leo awoke normally and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor.
At 71 years old, Leo is relatively young for a pope – and remains physically active. He works out weekly, including regular tennis matches with his personal secretary and enjoys riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat.
Leo has not been known to smoke, but there is a history of cancer in the pope's family. On Tuesday, the Vatican announced that Leo's older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, is currently hospitalized with a form of cancer. And Leo's mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990 at age 77. Back in 1984, while living in Rome, the future pope wrote to several friends saying, "my mother continues to undergo chemotherapy treatments. … She's a tough lady and handles it all well, which makes it a little easier for me being so far from Chicago."
The Vatican says the Pope has essentially cleared his public schedule for the next several days, until at least October 20. The Vatican has yet to announce any further treatments.

articles.title_orig: Drones hit ships in Black Sea, sinking 1 and prompting rescue operations, Bulgaria says
articles.title_zh: Drones hit ships in Black Sea, sinking 1 and prompting rescue operations, Bulgaria says
articles.content_orig:
Eleven sailors are missing following a drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian officials, prompting the country’s government to summon the Russian ambassador.
Overnight there were two attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials said, with one Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship, the “HS Dignity,” being sunk 15 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets – leading to an urgent search and rescue operation.
The search for the missing crew members – believed to be Syrian and Egyptian nationals – is still ongoing as of Tuesday afternoon, the Bulgarian Interior Ministry told CNN. Five people in the 16-person crew had already been rescued by other merchant vessels, the ministry said.
Another cargo ship called the “Chelsea 3,” which sails under the Maltese flag but is Ukrainian-owned, was struck by three drones as it sailed off the coast of Byala, Bulgaria.
Bulgarian border police said they rescued the entire crew of that vessel, which included seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, some of whom were injured in the attack. All were safely transported to the port of Varna, where the injured crew members received medical assistance, authorities said.
The country’s president and prime minister both strongly condemned the attacks in the vicinity of Bulgarian waters, which they indicated were likely connected to Russia.
“Bulgaria continues to seek support for an investigation into the attacks to determine the country of origin of the drones,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in a social media post on Tuesday.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side. However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation,” Radev added. “I will therefore summon the Russian Ambassador for a meeting today.”
Russian authorities did not immediately comment on the incidents. CNN has reached out to the Russian Embassy in Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, for comment.
Radev added that he informed NATO allies and the European Union of the attacks, as Bulgaria seeks assistance to strengthen air and maritime surveillance and defense.
“I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast,” she said. “Those responsible should be held accountable.”
“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable,” European Commission President Ursula von Der Leyen said in a statement, condemning the attack without explicitly mentioning Russia.
The latest attacks come after two ships were attacked by marine and aerial drones last week inside Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One of those vessels was damaged and the crew were all rescued, Bulgaria’s prime minister said at the time. A second vessel sank after being attacked and the search operation for the 10-person crew was eventually called off.
Attacks in the Black Sea have also heightened fears about global food security, as Ukraine is one of the world’s largest exports of grain.
Russia has repeatedly bombed Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, forcing the country to rely on shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO member states Bulgaria and Romania, as well as on Danube river ports. Meanwhile, Ukraine has also stepped up its attacks on Russian grain-exporting ships.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul condemned Tuesday’s strikes on merchant vessels near Bulgaria, calling them “an attack on international shipping & on global food security, depriving the most vulnerable of much-needed supplies” in a post on X.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that the alliance “will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea” and has “already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank.”
A CNN analysis of vessels near where the “HS Dignity” was sunk found that a NATO warship belonging to the Bulgarian Navy appears to be assisting in the search and rescue operations.
In a statement, the Syrian Seafarers’ Union expressed its “deep concern over the fate of the crew members who are still being searched for.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Eyad Kourdi and Thomas Gould contributed to this report.

The tournament, scheduled for August 20 through September 5, 2027, will bring 32 national teams together across the United States and Canada, with Omaha selected as one of the American host cities.
Omaha's Sports Commission 's Emily Winckler sat down with KETV NewsWatch 7’s Edward Moody to discuss what hosting the international competition means for Omaha and its growing reputation as a destination for women’s volleyball.
The city has built a strong reputation for women’s volleyball, fueled by Nebraska's success , the popularity of the professional Omaha Supernovas , and a fan base that has consistently turned out for major matches.
The 2027 competition will also carry significant implications for international volleyball, serving as part of the qualification pathway for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
Under the tournament’s new format, the highest-ranked teams that have not already qualified will have an opportunity to secure Olympic berths.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly Guilfoyle Resigns as Ambassador to Greece
articles.title_zh: Kimberly Guilfoyle Resigns as Ambassador to Greece
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Monday he is considering dismissing Kimberly Guilfoyle from her position as US ambassador to Greece after a string of reports about alleged misconduct, saying he is “not happy” about the situation.
“We’re looking at it — yeah. We’re not happy,” Trump told reporters when asked if he is considering firing her.
Trump has been monitoring reports claiming Guilfoyle, who was engaged to Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr. for four years, accepted lavish gifts as ambassador and sought money in exchange for providing access to administration figures before she was confirmed. CNN reported Sunday that the president has been weighing whether to dismiss her, with a personal familiar saying he was expected to decide soon.
Lawyers for Guilfoyle have denied the allegations about seeking money and said reports about her travel were misleading, adding that she complied with federal gift and reporting requirements.
The State Department’s Office of the Inspector General (OIG) is investigating Guilfoyle amid the misconduct allegations, a source familiar with the effort told CNN Monday.
The OIG’s press office did not respond to a request for comment. The office does not typically comment on ongoing investigations.
“As a matter of policy, OIG does not confirm, deny, or comment on investigative matters,” a State OIG spokesperson told CNN last week.
The reports about Guilfoyle have irked senior administration officials , particularly since they emerged when Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting Athens for a high-profile speech on Western democracy delivered from the Acropolis.
The president offered no defense of Guilfoyle when questioned by CNN about the allegations Friday.
“I just heard about it. Too bad. I mean, I don’t know,” Trump said. “I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice.”
CNN has reached out to the White House for comment.
Eric Deters, a former Trump donor, said Guilfoyle asked him in a text message to wire her $100,000 to pay off an American Express card in the days before her Senate confirmation. Deters ultimately did not wire Guilfoyle the money, saying he didn’t have the liquid assets at the time.
The messages were first reported by the Wall Street Journal .
Lawyers for the ambassador said in a statement provided to CNN that Deters owed Guilfoyle money for speeches and consulting work and called his statements false.
“When Ms. Guilfoyle was preparing to leave private life for public service, she did what any professional does and tried to close out her outstanding receivables. Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption,” her lawyers wrote.
Guilfoyle also denied to administration officials last week that she sent the messages, the person familiar said.
Guilfoyle has remained close to the Trump family. After her breakup with Donald Trump Jr., she received the plum assignment in Greece.
Allies of the president and his son told CNN they felt the episode is embarrassing, though it’s not clear whether there will be consequences for Guilfoyle. Trump has repeatedly made clear he is not happy when allies profit off of their relationship with him.
On Monday, Deters told CNN he had not been contacted by the inspector general’s office but said he had reached out to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to say he plans to sue Guilfoyle for defamation, after her lawyers disputed the authenticity of messages that she allegedly sent him. He did not get a response, he said.
“This problem is not getting any better for them,” Deters told CNN of the Trump administration. “I am going to sue her and her lawyers for defamation for claiming that her text messages were fake. Then they will have a lawsuit, she will have the committees looking at her, and the news media.”
CNN asked the White House for comment on Deters’ plans to sue.
Vice President JD Vance on Friday withheld judgment on whether there should be consequences for Guilfoyle, saying he refused to “try people in the court of public opinion.”
But the vice president said, in general, he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes. “Of course I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” he said.
“Let’s see what the truth is. And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Betsy Klein contributed to this report.

UNESCO works with governments and education stakeholders to strengthen the recognition, support and conditions that enable teachers to thrive.
As Artificial Intelligence (AI) transforms education and the teaching profession, UNESCO is supporting countries in strengthening teachers’ digital and AI competencies, including through the adoption and implementation of UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Teachers .
The joint Ministerial Statement on Education in the Age of AI , adopted at UNESCO on 8 September 2026, emphasizes that AI must support rather than replace teachers' professional contribution and judgement. The statement calls on countries to strengthen teacher agency through investment in teacher preparation and professional development, while ensuring that teachers play an active role in decisions regarding the use of AI systems in classrooms.

articles.title_orig: Save The World’s Rivers submits formal Stagecoach Mountain Ranch comments to Routt County planners
articles.title_zh: Save The World’s Rivers submits formal Stagecoach Mountain Ranch comments to Routt County planners
articles.content_orig:
jcoccaro@steamboatpilot.com
Save The World’s Rivers , a Colorado-based river conservation nonprofit, has submitted formal comments to the Routt County Planning Department on Discovery Land Company’s Stagecoach Mountain Ranch application, with the organization’s remarks limited squarely to the proposed development’s impacts on water.
In a six-page comment letter dated Oct. 7 , Save The World’s Rivers Executive Director Gary Wockner asked county planners to require a comprehensive list of documents and analyses from Discovery Land Company that demonstrate full compliance with the legal standards mandated for the project.
The nonprofit’s programs, Save The Colorado and Save The Poudre, work to protect and restore rivers within the Colorado River Basin, including the Yampa River.
Stagecoach Mountain Ranch is a 6,100-acre proposed private ski area and luxury residential development near Stagecoach Reservoir in South Routt County. Plans for the development include 613 luxury units alongside 137 workforce housing units, with 95 units marked for affordable housing accessible to the public.
Wockner’s letter comes approximately two months after the Routt County Planning Department submitted its second corrections letter to Discovery Land Company on its proposal , identifying more than 120 questions, conflicts and missing materials to be resolved before the county completes its review of the project’s 10 pending land-use applications.
Wockner began the letter by stating that the applicant’s current record of adequate water supply does not meet state standards and that Discovery Land Company’s current demand figures conflict.
The Stagecoach Mountain Ranch website, he wrote, lists potable water demand of 365 acre-feet per year and snowmaking demand of 275 acre-feet per year — yet according to the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District, the developers said in May 2025 that snowmaking would need approximately 400 acre-feet annually.
“The county should require one reconciled number, prepared by a registered engineer, before making any adequacy determination,” wrote Wockner, who added that the demand estimate “rests on an assumption the county cannot enforce.”
Discovery Land Company’s potable water estimate assumes that second homeowners occupy their homes 20-25 days a year, with demand calculated at 50% occupancy. Occupancy patterns, however, change based on ownership, remote work and short-term rentals, argued Wockner.
“If occupancy rises, demand rises with it,” he wrote. “An adequacy finding built on low occupancy is only valid if the county also caps actual use.”
On water sources, the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District, wrote Wockner, states that it has not received an application for a storage contract, and that no infrastructure currently exists to deliver reservoir water to the location of the ski area.
“The county should require a hydrogeologic analysis of the Browns Park wells, including whether the water is tributary to the Yampa and, if so, how depletions will be replace,” he wrote.
Drought conditions are the test for water supply, Wockner added — not the exception.
He requested that county planners require a reconciled report modeling dry-year yield, condition any approval on binding annual and daily caps for potable and snowmaking use, and require meters, public annual reporting and “mandatory curtailment of snowmaking in dry years.”
Wockner noted that as of Jan. 1, per state law, the county cannot allow the installation or placement of “nonfunctional turf, artificial turf or invasive plants in new development on commercial, institutional, industrial or common-interest-community property.”
The Stagecoach Mountain Ranch commercial base area, its proposed community marketplace and homeowners association-owned common areas, he said, fall within that prohibition.
Wockner referred to comments submitted by the Western Resilience Center in mid-September , which cites noteworthy commitments in Discovery Land Company’s sustainability plan and climate action plan strategy for the development.
Like Western Resilience, Save The World’s Rivers wonders to what extent they will become a “binding and enforceable component” of the final design and operation.
“Unless the County writes them into the approval, they will not,” wrote Wockner, who asked the county to convert every conservation commitment into a condition of approval, plat note and recorded covenant naming Routt County as a third-party beneficiary with enforcement rights.
Wockner was particularly blunt on the issue of water quality in Stagecoach Reservoir.
“Stagecoach Reservoir is not a healthy baseline that (Stagecoach Mountain Ranch) might degrade,” he wrote. “It is already in trouble.”
According to a 2025 monitoring report from the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District, chlorophyll-a at every reservoir site from late August through November 2025 exceeded both the cold-water aquatic life and direct-use water supply standards.
Cyanobacteria in the reservoir peaked between 50,000-60,000 cells/mL in September 2025, a level the report associated with “moderate-to-high recreational health risk,” with the bacteria’s dominant genus capable of producing toxins.
Additionally, the Yampa River immediately above and below the reservoir is on the state’s list of impaired waters for temperature.
“The wastewater plant is the crux,” wrote Wockner. All sewage from Stagecoach Mountain Ranch would go to the Morrison Creek Metropolitan Water and Sanitation District’s plant, which discharges directly into the reservoir.
Wockner noted that the plant’s discharge permit, issued in 2015, has expired, and that its renewal must account for effluent standards adopted since 2015.
Save The World’s Rivers is requesting a permit renewal that meets current standards; a phased schedule tying plat approvals to completed and funded wastewater capacity such that “units never outrun treatment”; and a binding “no net increase” nutrient commitment for total phosphorus and nitrogen reaching the reservoir, verified by applicant-funded monitoring conducted by either the district or a third party.
The nonprofit is further requesting a long-term performance guarantee that would compel Stagecoach Mountain Ranch to fund and execute remediation should reservoir water quality degrade — backed by escrowed funds and a revenue-based impact fund — as well as the prohibition of treated effluent in snowmaking, noted as illegal in Colorado.
Wockner joined Western Resilience in asking the county to strictly apply its “unavoidable encroachment” provision, noting that any encroachment should be presumed avoidable and that the applicant should bear the burden of proving otherwise.
The project website states that Discovery Land Company’s stormwater measures will cut phosphorus by 50-70% and nitrogen by 55%, and promises monitoring. Such figures should serve as enforceable performance standards, argued Wockner — not marketing.
“The applicant claims snowmaking on north-facing slopes will deliver colder water later in the melt season,” wrote Wockner. “That is a hypothesis, not a finding.”
Snowmaking, he continued, also loses water to evaporation and sublimation. He suggested the county require a hydrologic analysis of how snowmaking diversions and altered melt timing could affect flows and temperature in the relevant segments of the Yampa River.
“The Upper Yampa is already telling us its limits. The tailwater has been closed to fishing since October 2025,” wrote Wockner at the close of his comments. “The river above and below the dam is listed as impaired.”
“Into this system, SMR proposes roughly 750 residences, a private ski area with snowmaking, and a wastewater load that the existing plant cannot carry at buildout,” he continued.
Routt County, Wockner wrote, must “make every promise of conservation and water-quality protection binding, funded and enforceable before the first plat is recorded.” If Discovery Land Company cannot meet such standards, the county, he

articles.title_orig: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties and Adds Sexual Assault Investigators
articles.title_zh: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties and Adds Sexual Assault Investigators
articles.content_orig:
The Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell University's campus on Oct. 11, 2026, in Ithaca, New York.
Cornell University said on Tuesday that it is barring fraternity houses from hosting parties for the remainder of the academic year in an effort “to strengthen campus safety” after the school faced widespread backlash over its handling of an alleged gang rape by fraternity members in 2024.
Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff announced the news in a letter addressed to the campus community, which said that the ban will be effective immediately. He also outlined ways that the university would work to improve how it handles allegations of sexual assault in the future. In addition to strengthening campus safety, he addressed the need to provide better support to survivors—which involves allowing the New York State Police to independently investigate sexual assault allegations—and change the social culture at the university.
Cornell did not respond to questions about how the new measures would be implemented or tracked, but referred TIME to its FAQ page regarding the 2024 incident.
The announcement comes about a month after a woman, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against several entities, including Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity, and seven members of Chi Phi that she alleges sexually assaulted her in 2024. The case has made national headlines , and many people have criticized how Cornell and local authorities handled the incident. Hundreds of students and staff members held a protest on campus earlier this month, with some calling for Kotlikoff to resign and others chanting phrases like “Ban the frats!”
Read More: After the Cornell Case, Should Colleges Ban Fraternities?
In his letter on Tuesday, Kotlikoff addressed the backlash, saying that his conversations with various members of the campus community and the campus protests “have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.”
“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
Amid mounting pressure, Cornell’s Board of Trustees announced earlier this month that Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general, will lead an independent review into how the school handled the case. Kotlikoff also addressed the review in his letter, but said “it is clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action.” Cooperation with the New York State Police would coincide with the independent review; Kotlikoff said in his letter that investigators will interview survivors who decide to pursue criminal charges and “prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency.”
Kotlikoff said that Interfraternity Council houses will be barred from holding parties and social events, which “will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.” He added that the university will have a “zero tolerance” policy if fraternities violate the new rule, and that any fraternity that hosts “an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension.” Cornell has previously said that the Chi Phi fraternity on campus "was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus."
Other measures that Kotlikoff announced include strengthening support for survivors, such as by adding staffers to the Cornell Office of Civil Rights, and “changing the social culture at Cornell” through several initiatives, such as enhancing “existing education and programming to address the bystander effect.”
“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors. Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

articles.title_orig: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
articles.title_zh: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump and his advisers are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, with Trump having remarked privately that he did not initially know that Nidal Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down, two sources familiar with the discussions told CNN.
The president was not aware that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was announcing last week that the administration planned to let the public watch the execution, the sources said, and was not sure what to make of it at first. Trump was, however, firmly behind the decision to execute Hasan via firing squad , multiple officials told CNN, and he’s often defended it in public.
And even after Hegseth posted on X on Thursday confirming that the Pentagon planned to livestream the execution, Trump polled several of his advisers and allies about how to proceed.
It was during the those conversations that Trump learned Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down — he was shot in the back by law enforcement during the 2009 shooting at Ford Hood — and that he now uses a wheelchair, the sources said, which made showing the execution publicly less palatable to the president.
One of the sources familiar with the discussions pointed to Trump’s deep understanding of imagery as a key reason why he may decide to ditch plans for the livestream. The president has also listened to the argument that a public execution by firing squad could serve as propaganda for foreign adversaries and terrorists to try to paint Hasan as a martyr, a Trump adviser told CNN.
The White House on Tuesday referred CNN to the president’s comments on Saturday in which he acknowledged “two thoughts” about what to do and said he’d make the ultimate decision.
“He was vicious. He was violent,” Trump told reporters about Hasan over the weekend. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So, I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
The Pentagon is also reevaluating plans to fully livestream the execution, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Even if there is a broadcast of the event, the source said, it will likely be cut before shots are fired, in part, due to concerns that the moment could offer a propaganda opportunity for terrorist groups.
Hegseth’s office has not responded to additional requests for comment about whether plans to livestream the execution have changed.
The plan to livestream the execution has faced bipartisan backlash, and people across the Pentagon and the Army were caught off guard, CNN has previously reported .
Trump told reporters on Friday that he was not involved but said, “I understand the decision,” adding that some people “want to set an example” by livestreaming the execution.
Hegseth had initially recommended death by firing squad for Hasan — who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others — and Trump approved it.
The execution, which is scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the US Army’s first such execution of a soldier since World War II and its first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years.
A US-born citizen of Palestinian descent, Hasan said he was targeting soldiers he was set to deploy with to Afghanistan and wanted to protect the Taliban and its leaders from the US military.
CNN’s Zachary Cohen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases exceed 9,000 as containment efforts falter - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases exceed 9,000 as containment efforts falter - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Confirmed Ebola cases have surpassed 9,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) outbreak, according to Health Ministry data, as efforts to stifle transmission falter.
The ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths on Tuesday – a death toll of nearly half the known cases.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history. Globally, the toll is only second to the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 confirmed cases and more than 11,000 deaths across Guinea, ⁠⁠Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccines or treatments and has raised concerns over cross-border transmission.
Last week, Kenya reported its first imported case in which a Kenyan national who lived in the DRC travelled through Uganda before reaching Nairobi, where he died.
Uganda also reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but the country was declared Ebola-free in August.
The current outbreak in the DRC was announced in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February. The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.
Efforts to contain the virus face obstacles as health workers and other responders in the DRC face mistrust in local communities, with many believing the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money . The outbreak is also occurring amid an ongoing conflict between the M23 rebel group and government forces, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.
A local politician in eastern DRC was beaten to death in September after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio, according to his political party.
A clinical trial to evaluate vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain is being prepared for the DRC in the coming weeks, WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu said on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Real-World, First-Line IO-Based Combos Are Associated With Improved OS vs TKI Monotherapy in Advanced RCC
articles.title_zh: Real-World, First-Line IO-Based Combos Are Associated With Improved OS vs TKI Monotherapy in Advanced RCC
articles.content_orig:
First-line IO-based combination regimens were increasingly used and associated with longer observed survival in advanced renal cell carcinoma.
First-line immuno-oncology (IO)–based combination regimens, particularly IO plus a TKI, were associated with improved overall survival (OS) compared with TKI monotherapy in a real-world cohort of patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC), according to findings from a retrospective real-world study presented at the 2026 Kidney Cancer Research Summit . 1,2
Findings showed that at a median follow-up of 13.9 months, the median OS in the overall population (n = 2123) was 34.7 months. 1 Notably, the median OS was 44.1 months among patients who received an IO-TKI combination (n = 987) compared with 32.8 months for those given an IO-IO combination (n = 746) and 29.8 months for patients given TKI monotherapy (n = 390).
Notably, from 2019 to 2024, the proportion of patients receiving an IO-TKI combination increased from 33.8% to 48.6%, whereas IO-IO decreased from 40.5% to 34.5% and TKI monotherapy decreased from 25.7% to 16.9%.
“The advanced RCC treatment landscape continues to evolve toward IO-based combinations in [the] first line and continued TKI monotherapy in later lines,” lead study author Neil J. Shah, MBBS, and colleagues wrote in the poster. “While health care resource utilization [HCRU] and costs remain substantial, these results underscore both the clinical progress achieved and the ongoing opportunity to optimize resource use in advanced RCC care.”
Shah is an assistant attending physician and genitourinary medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, New York.
Investigators conducted a retrospective cohort study using Optum’s deidentified Clinformatics Data Mart Database, with the database period extended from January 1, 2017, through December 31, 2024, and included commercially insured and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.
Eligible adults had at least 2 claims with an RCC diagnosis, evidence of secondary metastasis, and initiation of a National Comprehensive Cancer Network–recommended first-line systemic regimen on or after April 19, 2019. Patients were categorized according to whether they received IO-TKI, IO-IO, or TKI monotherapy.
Investigators evaluated outcomes included treatment patterns, treatment sequencing, OS, all-cause and advanced RCC–related HCRU, and costs. OS was estimated using an unadjusted Kaplan-Meier analysis, and HCRU and costs were calculated on a per-patient-per-month (PPPM) basis.
The mean age of the overall population was 68.1 years (standard deviation [SD], 9.6), and the median age was 69.0 years (interquartile range [IQR], 63.0-75.0). The respective mean ages were 67.4, 68.2, and 69.5 years in the IO-TKI, IO-IO, and TKI monotherapy groups. Men comprised 70.9% of the overall population, including 71.6%, 72.8%, and 65.6% of the respective treatment cohorts.
Overall, 50.2% of patients were non-Hispanic White, 7.3% were non-Hispanic Black, 13.6% were Hispanic, and 2.2% were Asian; race or ethnicity was unknown for 26.7% of patients. Most patients lived in the South (45.1%), followed by the Midwest (25.1%), West (19.5%), and Northeast (10.3%).
Medicare Advantage covered 71.1% of the study population, and 28.9% had commercial insurance. The proportion covered by Medicare Advantage was highest in the TKI-monotherapy group at 78.7%, compared with 71.0% in the IO-IO group and 68.1% in the IO-TKI group.
Additional data showed that 32.3% of patients remained on their initial treatment, 29.0% advanced to second-line therapy, and 18.7% died. Another 20.0% discontinued treatment without a recorded death or subsequent therapy.
TKI monotherapy was the most frequently used treatment class in both the second- and third-line settings. Among patients who received second-line therapy, 47.2% received TKI monotherapy compared with 23.1% who received IO-TKI, 9.3% who received IO monotherapy, 7.6% who received a TKI plus an mTOR inhibitor, 7.0% who received IO-IO, and 5.8% who received another regimen.
In the third-line setting, 42.1% of patients received TKI monotherapy, 18.8% received IO-TKI, and 14.2% received a TKI plus an mTOR inhibitor; other treatments were administered to 15.2% of patients.
Overall, 61.3% of patients had at least 1 inpatient admission, including 57.6% treated with first-line IO-TKI, 66.6% treated with IO-IO, and 60.5% treated with TKI monotherapy. The median PPPM inpatient admissions was 0.1 overall. Median lengths of stay were 1.0 day with IO-TKI, 1.1 days with IO-IO, and 1.3 days with TKI monotherapy.
At least 1 emergency department visit was reported for 64.1% of patients, whereas 99.8% had at least 1 outpatient visit. The median number of outpatient visits PPPM was 5.4 overall, including 5.5 with IO-TKI, 5.6 with IO-IO, and 4.3 with TKI monotherapy.
Median total health care costs PPPM were $32,829 overall, $38,408 with IO-TKI, $30,484 with IO-IO, and $24,098 with TKI monotherapy.
Median medical costs PPPM were highest with IO-IO at $26,589, compared with $21,800 for IO-TKI and $7462 for TKI monotherapy. Conversely, median pharmacy costs were $15,871 with IO-TKI, $15,103 with TKI monotherapy, and $415 with IO-IO. Investigators noted that the oral administration of TKIs may have contributed to higher pharmacy costs, whereas intravenously administered IO agents may have contributed to higher medical costs.

articles.title_orig: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
articles.title_zh: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Regulators fined Bank of America ( BAC ) more than $1.2 billion on Tuesday over widespread failures in the banking giant's safeguards against money laundering and other illicit financial activity.
The Treasury Department said the nation's second-largest bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including transactions potentially tied to Chinese money-laundering networks, narcotics trafficking, and fraud.
The enforcement actions include a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the third-largest fine in the Treasury Department's history after it fined crypto exchange Binance $3.4 billion in 2023 and TD Bank for $1.3 billion in 2024. The fine also includes a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the largest ever imposed by that regulator.
The OCC penalty will be credited against FinCEN's assessment rather than added to it. Separately, a $11.6 million sanctions settlement brings the total penalties to more than $1.21 billion.
"Even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Bank of America's stock fell more than 2% after markets closed on Tuesday. It reports third quarter earnings Wednesday morning.
The bank said it will include a "non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share" in its third quarter results.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," a Bank of America spokesperson said in an email statement, adding that the Charlotte, North Carolina based lender has invested "billions of dollars in technology" and dedicated "thousands of employees to combat financial crime" to resolve the deficiencies.
Regulators said Bank of America's failures extended across its transaction monitoring systems, customer due diligence, and internal oversight.
The bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including over $1 billion involving national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.
FinCEN said Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act and had effectively outsourced substantial portions of its suspicious activity detection responsibilities to law enforcement and other financial institutions.
The bank also prioritized revenue over compliance resources, according to Treasury, allowing suspicious transactions to go uninvestigated for extended periods.
The penalties come nearly two years after Bank of America agreed to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring it to address longstanding weaknesses in its anti-money laundering controls.
The OCC said the bank failed to make sufficient progress despite that earlier enforcement action.
"Bank of America's poor response to its [Bank Secrecy Act] deficiencies is unacceptable," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, describing continued breakdowns in internal controls.
Separately, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced an $11.6 million settlement involving 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Iran, and other countries and activities.
As part of the latest enforcement actions, Bank of America must conduct a review of previously undetected suspicious transactions with an outside party and undergo independent assessments of its compliance controls.
David Hollerith covers a range of developments throughout the financial sector, from Wall Street to banking and asset management to crypto and fintech. Email him at david.hollerith@yahoofinance.com. Follow him on X at @DsHollers.

articles.title_orig: China Spooked Memory Stocks. Investors Picked Their Losers.
articles.title_zh: China Spooked Memory Stocks. Investors Picked Their Losers.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
China rattled the memory trade on Tuesday. But by the close, investors had made up their minds about who actually has a problem. It's the DRAM makers.
ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's biggest memory chipmaker, said over the weekend it had made real progress on a new chip design that crams more data into less space, CNBC reports. Asia took it badly: SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in Seoul and Samsung fell over 7%.
U.S. memory stocks opened in the same hole, with nearly every name down 5% to 8%. Then the buyers showed up.
Seagate, Western Digital and SanDisk clawed back almost all of it and closed down less than 2%. Micron didn't get the same rescue. It finished down 3.6%, its second straight loss. SK Hynix's U.S. shares fell 3.2%. The S&P 500 ended flat.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
The split makes sense. CXMT makes DRAM, the same chips Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung sell. A Chinese rival closing the gap is a direct shot at their pricing. Hard drives and flash storage are a different business.
Some analysts think the market overreacted. Rayliant's Phillip Wool told CNBC that CXMT still hasn't shown it can produce at scale, and it isn't a threat yet in the high-bandwidth memory chips that power AI. He said the selloff showed "how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment."
Still, the CXMT news looks more like an excuse than a cause. Memory stocks were already well off their highs before the weekend, with Micron down about a quarter from its peak and Western Digital down by half. Investors have been hunting for a reason to take profits on the AI trade's biggest winners. China handed them one, and they used it on the stocks with the most to lose.

articles.title_orig: A Father’s Mission Is to Show the World ‘What Russia Did to My Family’
articles.title_zh: A Father’s Mission Is to Show the World ‘What Russia Did to My Family’
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Alaska on Aug. 15, 2025.
President Donald Trump is facing growing backlash over his plan to import diesel from Russia , with some Republican and Democratic lawmakers insisting that the controversial deal “violates” the law.
Congress four years ago passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act , which prohibits U.S. imports of Russian-origin energy products covered by Chapter 27 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule , including diesel. Democratic Rep. Lloyd Doggett of Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, argued Monday that Trump is “directly violating that law” by “lifting sanctions to permit the first Russian diesel imports into the United States since the law took effect, without satisfying the specific legal conditions it requires.”
He suggested the lack of congressional oversight on Trump’s deal with Putin renders it unlawful, and noted how the plan showcases a sharp turn from Washington, as it comes just weeks after Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The sanctions bill was named after Lindsey Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
“Russia can [now] export fossil fuel to the U.S. after Trump violated the specific provisions of a federal statute,” Doggett said on Tuesday in a statement to TIME. “While offering little benefit for Americans, this unlawful action will provide substantial new funding for Putin‘s war machine to continue murdering Ukrainian civilians.”
Doggett’s concerns match those of Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who told NBC’s Meet the Press over the weekend that he believes “there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law.”
Tillis was one of seven Senators who publicly urged the Administration on Sunday to “immediately reverse course” on the agreement announced Friday, arguing that it goes against the 2022 law.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” read the statement co-signed by Republican Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute,” they said.
In a letter sent to Trump on Tuesday, Tillis, Collins, and Murkowski, were joined by fellow Republican Senators Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, John Cornyn of Texas, and Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma alongside six Democratic Senators as they told the President the deal “is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies [and] should be rescinded.” The letter came a day after Trump publicly dismissed the criticism stemming from within his own party.
"Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he told reporters at the White House. “Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like.”
Trump’s deal to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets comes as he faces growing political pressure ahead of the November midterms. Spiraling energy costs have become a key concern for voters, threatening to undermine Republican efforts to maintain their majorities in Congress. The financial upheaval has meant that Trump risks losing his hold on farm country . However, experts are skeptical that an influx of Russian fuel will bring relief to struggling Americans, given how short the supply is due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
While some lawmakers also predict the impact on American consumers will be slight , the key sticking point for many centers on whether Trump’s diesel deal with Putin violates the 2022 law, with some Republicans and Democrats insisting that Trump is pushing the limits of presidential authority. Here’s what to know about the debate—and where legal experts stand on the matter.
While Presidents typically have broad authority to waive sanctions, Congress placed specific limits on that power in the April 2022 legislation, says Kristen Eichensehr, a professor of law at Harvard Law School.
“In many sanctions authorities, the President has broad authority to waive imposition of the sanctions or to issue licenses that basically provide an exception to the sanctions,” she tells TIME. “The [2022 act] is an unusual law, given how careful and specific Congress was in providing that the President lacks that flexibility.”
Under Section 3 of the legislation, the President must first consult with the House Ways and Means and Foreign Affairs Committees, along with the Senate Finance and Foreign Relations Committees, and submit a report at least 45 days before providing the required certification.
Lawmakers have argued that the Administration has failed to follow this process.
“The President has to provide a certification to Congress in advance before lifting the prohibition,” says Eichensehr, pointing to the specific criteria set out in the wording of the law.
The law requires a determination by the President to Congress that the Russian Federation has withdrawn and ceased hostilities accepted by Ukraine; poses no immediate threat to any NATO member; and recognizes the right of the Ukrainian people to freely and independently choose their own government.
But Eichensehr insists that these are “not certifications that the President could make at the current moment” because “none of those things have happened, and that's the main restriction in the law.”
Even if all these conditions were met, the legislation would still require the President to wait an additional 90 days before the termination of the import ban could take effect, during which, Congress could enact a joint resolution of disapproval.
“On the substance, the President cannot, as a factual matter, make the certifications because Russia is still attacking Ukraine,” says Eichensehr. “As a procedural matter, [because he reportedly has not consulted Congress], he hasn't followed the process that the law sets out.”
Edward Swaine, a research professor at George Washington University Law School, suggests these restrictions were put in place to ensure that “when the President and the Treasury Secretary decide that circumstances have changed, they go back and explain this to Congress, and give it notice so that it can disagree.”
“The President is supposed to make this determination that Russia has withdrawn its forces and doesn't pose any further threat of aggression. These are fairly high standards,” he tells TIME, noting that the statue provides “Congress with adequate notice to allow it to generate a joint resolution of disapproval.”
“They don't want the President to be able to change this regime on a whim, and so I imagine Congress looking at this action and justifiably thinking that this is inconsistent,” he adds.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the legality of the agreement, insisting that the Trump Administration is acting within its existing legal authority to help bring energy prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News on Sunday, without elaborating on which legal authorities he was referring to.
On Friday, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including its importation, until April 7, 2027.

articles.title_orig: David Cromer Will Direct Peter Friedman in Hanukkah Spectacular World Premiere
articles.title_zh: David Cromer Will Direct Peter Friedman in Hanukkah Spectacular World Premiere
articles.content_orig:
Max Posner's comedy will begin at the Woolly Mammoth Theatre in November.
October 13, 2026 By Andrew Gans
Washington , D.C.'s Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company will present the world premiere of Hanukkah Spectacular , a new comedy by Lucille Lortel Award nominee Max Posner, beginning November 14.
Directed by Tony winner David Cromer ( The Band's Visit , Dead Outlaw , The Sound Inside ), performances will continue through December 13.
Stage and screen star and Tony nominee Peter Friedman ( Succession, Ragtime , JOB ) will lead a cast that also includes Laura Heisler , Ben Edelman , Ben Beckley , and Ethan J. Miller.
Set over a long weekend at a Midtown talent agency, Hanukkah Spectacular follows a group of Jewish artists brought together to create a commercially viable holiday hit about Hanukkah.
“The first time I saw a reading of Hanukkah Spectacular three years ago, I knew I had just experienced something unforgettable, and I’m so lucky to get to share its world premiere with D.C. this holiday season,” says Woolly Mammoth Artistic Director Reggie D. White in a statement. “Seeing Max [Posner] and [David] Cromer collaborate feels like once-in-generation chemistry. Watching them amplify, interrogate, and deepen each other’s work is like you’re witnessing two brilliant artists write the book on collaboration in front of your very eyes. Max’s play is a hilarious and deeply recognizable story about a group of people trying to make something honest while figuring out what they actually believe. This production promises to be exactly the kind of work we come to the theatre to see: disarming, surprising, and so true that that it sends you back into the world thinking about your own life a little differently.”
Posner's play The Treasurer , also directed by Cromer, premiered at Playwrights Horizons and received a Lucille Lortel Award nomination for Best Play. He is a Sundance Institute Fellow, a recipient of the Helen Merrill Award and three MacDowell Fellowships, and was the 2024–25 Sun Valley Playwright-in-Residence at the Hemingway House.
